patient_case.prompt_question: A 15-year-old boy presents after an appendectomy 1 week ago with no symptoms except for amber-colored urine. His physical exam is normal and his urinalysis shows 3+ protein with no other abnormalities. A repeat urinalysis 3 days later is similar. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? Options: A. CT scan abdomen and pelvis with contrast; B. Renal biopsy; C. Repeat urinalysis; D. Urine dipstick in the morning and in the afternoon.
patient_case.note: This prompt originates from a clinical scenario; diagnosis or management is to be inferred.

branch.condition: Analyze each option based on known pathophysiology, presentation, and available clues
branch.interpretation: The patient is asymptomatic with isolated proteinuria that persists on repeat testing. The suspicion is for orthostatic proteinuria, common in adolescents. Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria presents with proteinuria during the day (upright posture) and resolves in the morning (after recumbency).

diagnostic_options.option: CT scan abdomen and pelvis with contrast
diagnostic_options.description: Advanced imaging used to evaluate anatomical abnormalities in the abdomen/pelvis.
evidence_for: Could evaluate for renal masses or structural anomalies if suspected
evidence_against: No symptoms or physical findings suggesting abdominal pathology
Unnecessary radiation exposure in an asymptomatic adolescent

diagnostic_options.description: Invasive procedure to evaluate glomerular pathology.
evidence_for: Indicated in suspected glomerulonephritis when accompanied by hematuria, hypertension, or declining renal function
evidence_against: Patient is asymptomatic with isolated proteinuria and normal exam
No evidence of active glomerular disease

diagnostic_options.description: Reassessment of urine protein levels to confirm persistence of proteinuria.
evidence_against: Repeat UA has already been performed and remains unchanged

diagnostic_options.option: Urine dipstick in the morning and in the afternoon
diagnostic_options.description: Evaluation for orthostatic proteinuria by comparing urine protein levels in recumbent versus upright positions.
evidence_for: Appropriate next step in an asymptomatic adolescent with isolated proteinuria
Distinguishes between orthostatic proteinuria and persistent pathologic proteinuria
evidence_against: None significant in this clinical context

reasoning_tree.conclusion: The most appropriate next step in management is to perform serial urine dipstick measurements in the morning and afternoon to evaluate for orthostatic proteinuria.
